newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-SLALOM QUEEN WIBERG DREAMS OF DOWNHILL.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SLALOM QUEEN WIBERG DREAMS OF DOWNHILL.

text.p: Most world champions put all their efforts into defending their titles.
This is not the case with Pernilla Wiberg, the 1996 slalom champion from Sierra Nevada who is more interested in claiming the only two gold medals missing from her collection in downhill and super-G.
The 26-year-old Swede has giant slalom golds from the 1991 world championships and 1992 Olympics, as well as combination titles from the 1994 Olympics and Sierra Nevada.
Nevertheless, "Pilla" is without doubt a hot favourite for Wednesday's night slalom under floodlights on the Kandahar piste.
She has won two World Cup slaloms this season and currently heads the discipline's standings.

"My goals this winter are to win the slalom World Cup because I have never won a crystal globe like that. But in Sestriere I want to win the downhill and super-G," she said in Cortina d'Ampezzo last month.
"I have never won a downhill. Sestriere would be the perfect place to do it," said Wiberg. "I am less concentrated on the slalom."
Unlike Wiberg, Austrian-born Claudia Riegler who races for her mother's country of New Zealand, has her sights firmly set on snatching gold in her only discipline.
Riegler made a strong start to the winter and won the first two World Cup slaloms. Her form wavered in January when she failed in Maribor and Zwiesel.
However, she gained a major boost by winning last Sunday's World Cup slalom in Laax.
"I've worked hard in the last two weeks to correct some technical problems," Salzburg-based Riegler said after her victory in Laax.
"I see now that I can be the best again and that's a better way to start the world championships than wondering if you can win."
No New Zealander has ever won a medal at an Alpine skiing world championships, although Annelise Coberger took a slalom silver at the 1992 Olympics and Riegler was fourth in Sierra Nevada.
Tough competition will come from Italians Lara Magoni and Olympic and world champion Deborah Compagnoni.
Compagnoni, the defending giant slalom champion, spent a lot of time training slalom over the summer months and claimed her first slalom victory in Semmering in December.
Magoni, a regular since 1992, reached the podium for the first time this winter with a third place in Maribor and second in Laax.
"I now believe it is possible to get on the podium in Sestriere," a confident Magoni said after Laax.
Others to watch are Austria's slalom World Cup title-holder Elfi Eder, France's 1996 silver medallist Patricia Chauvet and Switzerland's Sonja Nef.

Eder is determined to capture a medal, having lost her chance in Sierra Nevada with a poor second run. Chauvet has made two podium appearances this season, while Nef has the advantage of having won last year's World Cup night slalom here.

Missing in Sestriere is Slovenia's top woman skier Urska Hrovat. Hrovat, 1996 world championship slalom bronze medallist, tore a knee ligament in a World Cup giant slalom in Cortina D'Ampezzo two weeks ago.
